content: The health effects of tobacco use are profound and vary depending on the method of consumption (smoking, chewing, or snuffing) and the quantity used. Smoking, the most common form of tobacco use, is strongly associated with an increased risk of lung cancer and cardiovascular diseases. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated in 2002 that smoking was responsible for 26% of male deaths and 9% of female deaths in developed countries. Similarly, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has described tobacco use as the leading preventable risk to human health in developed nations and a major cause of premature death worldwide. Smokers, on average, live 5 to 10 years less than non-smokers, and approximately half of male smokers will die from smoking-related illnesses. WHO has projected that tobacco will claim one billion lives this century. The primary health risks associated with tobacco include diseases of the cardiovascular system, such as myocardial infarction (heart attack), respiratory diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and emphysema, and various cancers, particularly lung cancer, as well as cancers of the larynx, mouth, and pancreas. Smoking increases the risk of pancreatic cancer by 75%. Before World War I, lung cancer was considered rare, but the post-war rise in cigarette smoking led to an epidemic of lung cancer. Among individuals who have ever smoked, nearly one in ten will develop lung cancer, and one in six men who continue smoking will develop the disease. In contrast, only one in seventy-five lifelong non-smokers will develop lung cancer. Male smokers are also 85% more likely to experience impotence compared to non-smokers, with smoking being a significant cause of erectile dysfunction due to arterial narrowing. The risk of developing smoking-related diseases is directly proportional to the duration and intensity of smoking. However, cessation of smoking leads to a gradual reduction in these risks as the body begins to repair itself. Smoking-related diseases include various cancers (lung, kidney, larynx, head and neck, breast, bladder, esophagus, pancreas, stomach, and others), cardiovascular diseases (stroke, peripheral vascular disease), respiratory ailments (COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis), birth defects in offspring of pregnant smokers, Buerger's disease, cataracts, cognitive dysfunction (including increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease and brain atrophy), and impotence. Pipe and cigar smokers, while inhaling less smoke than cigarette smokers, still face significantly higher risks of lung cancer and cancers of the oral cavity, larynx, and esophagus compared to non-smokers. Chewing tobacco is also carcinogenic, particularly for cancers of the mouth and jaw. The benefits of smoking cessation are immediate. Blood pressure, heart rate, and body temperature return to normal ranges, the risk of heart attack decreases, sensory abilities like smell and taste improve, and circulation becomes more efficient. Nicotine, the primary addictive component of tobacco, is a stimulant that creates physical and psychological dependence. Despite the small amount of nicotine inhaled during smoking, it is sufficient to cause addiction. Nicotine is rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream, reaching the brain within 10 seconds, which reinforces the addictive behavior. Withdrawal symptoms, including irritability, jitteriness, dry mouth, rapid heartbeat, insomnia, and mild depression, can appear quickly due to nicotine's short half-life of about one hour. These symptoms can occur even in light or irregular smokers. While physical dependence on nicotine typically resolves within 10 to 20 days after cessation, psychological dependence may persist for months or years. Tobacco smoke contains approximately 3,000 chemicals, many of which are biologically active and harmful. Long-term exposure to compounds like carbon monoxide, cyanide, and others damages lung and arterial tissues, contributing to cardiovascular disease and loss of elasticity in the alveoli, leading to emphysema and COPD. Additionally, tobacco contains radioactive carcinogens such as lead-210 and polonium-210, which are deposited in the lungs and other tissues. These radioactive elements, absorbed from the soil and fertilizers used in tobacco cultivation, deliver significant radiation doses to lung tissue, increasing the risk of lung cancer. Polonium-210, for instance, emits high-energy alpha particles that cause extensive chromosomal damage when inhaled. Research suggests that the radioactive components of tobacco smoke may account for a significant proportion of smoking-related lung cancers. Tobacco smoke also contains over 19 known carcinogens, including polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and nitrosamines. PAHs, such as benzo[a]pyrene, are highly carcinogenic and mutagenic, forming permanent attachments to nuclear DNA and potentially leading to genetic mutations and cancer. Nitrosamines, formed during the curing process of tobacco leaves, are another group of potent carcinogens. Nicotine itself is not directly carcinogenic but may act as a synergistic carcinogen when combined with other harmful compounds in tobacco smoke. Genetic factors also play a role in nicotine addiction and smoking-related cancer risks. Studies have identified genetic variations on chromosome 15 that encode nicotine receptors, increasing susceptibility to addiction and lung cancer. Individuals with one copy of the mutation have a 30% higher risk of lung cancer, while those with two copies face an 80% increased risk. Smoking significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular disease by promoting arterial narrowing and blockages, leading to heart attacks and strokes. Young smokers under 40 are five times more likely to experience a heart attack compared to non-smokers. Smoking also has severe oral health consequences, including an increased risk of oral cancer, periodontal disease, tooth loss, and halitosis. Smokeless tobacco products cause gingival recession and mucosal lesions, while smoking is a major contributor to tooth staining and loss of taste sensation. Tobacco use during pregnancy poses significant risks to fetal health, including spontaneous abortion, low birth weight, and increased risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Secondhand smoke exposure is equally dangerous, increasing the risk of pregnancy loss and SIDS. Nicotine from smoking can also be transferred to infants through breast milk. There is no credible evidence that low tar or light cigarettes are safer than regular cigarettes. Similarly, while cigar smoking carries a lower risk of lung cancer compared to cigarette smoking, it still poses significant health risks, including cancers of the oral cavity, esophagus, and larynx. Pipe smoking also carries substantial risks, particularly for oral cancer. While tobacco has occasionally been reported to have isolated positive effects on certain medical conditions, these are far outweighed by its numerous and severe health risks.
